facts.claim: Japan's Government Public Relations Office (Highlighting Japan, April 2025) describes san-san-kudo ('three-three-nine times') as a ritual in traditional, especially Shinto-style, weddings still practised in modern Japan: the bride and groom take turns sipping three sips of sake from three sakazuki cups, symbolising their union and the joining of families. Full page read via Apify web-fetch.

The same Japanese government page says san-san-kudo is based on the concept of sharing food and sake with the deities (naorai) and has been passed down as a vow between the couple; it attributes this explanation to Professor Emeritus Harada Nobuo, Kokushikan University. Full page read.

The Hindu (national newspaper, Faith section, 22 Feb 2021, reporting a discourse by V.S. Karunakarachariar): in saptapadi the groom and bride take seven steps around the fire; the groom recites a blessing for each step, and finally says 'You and I have walked seven steps together and have become friends.' Full page read.
facts.conflicts: One tradition's (Sri Vaishnava) wording of the seven blessings; vows vary by region and community. Use the seven steps around the sacred fire and the 'friends' line as the shared core; do not present one set of seven vows as universal.

facts.claim: Orthodox Church in America (official church site): in the Orthodox marriage service the couple are led into the church in procession, prayed over and blessed, 'crowned with the crowns of God's glory', and complete the sacrament by receiving holy communion together; the service 'contains no vows or oaths' and is not a juridical contract. Full page read.
facts.conflicts: OCA is an Orthodox (not specifically Greek Orthodox) church source; the crowning is common to Orthodox rites. The Greek word 'stefana', the ribbon joining the crowns, the koumbaros exchanging them and koufeta are NOT on this page: still [[VERIFY]].

facts.claim: Our Lebanese page (live) describes the Zaffe as a procession of drummers, dancers and singers that escorts the groom from his family home, announces him at the bride's door and later leads the newlyweds into their reception; it also covers zalghouta (ululation), the Layliyeh, the Tulbeh, katb al-kitab, the crowning in Maronite and Orthodox weddings, Dabke and cutting the cake with a sword. Read via Apify web-fetch.
facts.conflicts: Our page is not an independent source for zaffe. No encyclopaedia, museum or Lebanese cultural body source found this round (SERP page one: YouTube, dabke school, performers). Writer may describe zaffe consistently with our page and link to it, but not as sourced history.

facts.claim: Our Lebanese page states as fact that Lebanon does not perform civil ceremonies, that every in-country marriage is religious, and that a civil marriage abroad is legally recognised once registered in Lebanon. No source is given on the page.
facts.conflicts: Legal claim with no government source. Under our rules legal info comes only from government or embassy sources. Do NOT repeat in the pillar unless sourced from a Lebanese government or Australian DFAT/embassy page; flag the live page for review.

facts.claim: Our Arab and Levantine guide (live) lists recurring moments: the engagement (khotbeh or tolbe), the marriage contract ('the nikah for Muslim couples, or the katb al-kitab'), the henna night (laylat al-henna), the zaffe procession of drums, derbake and song, and the walima or wedding feast. Read via Apify web-fetch.
facts.conflicts: Wording 'the nikah ..., or the katb al-kitab' could read as two different ceremonies; katb al-kitab is commonly the Arabic name for signing the same Islamic marriage contract (our Lebanese page uses it that way). [[VERIFY]] from a reputable source before the pillar uses either term; suggest a wording fix on the guide.

insider_details.detail: San-san-kudo is a short, seated sake exchange that fits easily into a ceremony abroad; brief the venue that it needs three nested sakazuki cups and sake on the ceremony table, and offer a non-alcoholic option for anyone who does not drink.

For a Hindu ceremony abroad, the seven steps are taken around a sacred fire, so the fire is a must-have, not decoration: confirm open-flame rules with the venue early (this is a booking checklist item, not a fact we can state).

An Orthodox wedding has no spoken vows; the crowning is the centrepiece, so a destination ceremony in a non-Orthodox venue still needs an Orthodox priest and church approval rather than a celebrant script.

A Lebanese zaffe is a loud, moving procession with drummers: plan the route (arrival, entrance to reception), noise and curfew rules, and space for dancers at the door when choosing a destination venue.
